tier_reason: First-party hyperfine tables in the README, regenerated by the public benches/update_readme.sh from .github/workflows/benchmark.yaml; the runner CPU model, the Rust toolchain version and the filtlong/seqtk versions are not stated, so not A. The JOSS paper (paper/paper.md) only repeats '21 and 1.2 times faster' with no methodology, so it does not lift the entry to B.

corrections.hardware: GitHub Actions runner pinned to ubuntu-24.04 in .github/workflows/benchmark.yaml (the README note says ubuntu-latest); CPU model not stated.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rasusa: cargo build --release with stable Rust (dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable, version unpinned); the release profile sets lto = true, strip = true. filtlong and seqtk come from bioconda through micromamba with unpinned versions; the current bioconda recipes (filtlong 0.3.1, seqtk 1.5) append -O3 in build.sh. hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10 (single) and --warmup 10 --runs 100 (paired).
corrections.caveats: First-party, on a shared GitHub Actions runner (CPU model not stated); the tool versions and Rust toolchain are not pinned. The 34.9x over filtlong is not like-for-like: filtlong scores every read by length and windowed quality and keeps the best subset, while rasusa draws a random subset. The rasusa JOSS paper itself says filtlong is a filtering tool, not a subsampler. For the same job, seqtk sample -2 (two-pass random sampling, the mode the README calls analogous), the result is parity: 0.950 s vs 0.963 s, 1.01x. Against seqtk's one-pass reservoir mode it is 1.19 +/- 0.14x. The README's internal v4.1.0 to v5.0.0 table (about 7-8% wall time, 25-74% peak RSS) compares rasusa with itself, not with a C/C++ tool.
corrections.why_faster: Against filtlong the gap is algorithmic: filtlong does per-read quality scoring while rasusa does random selection. Against seqtk -2, which uses the same two-pass random selection, there is no meaningful win (1.01x), so nothing here shows a Rust-over-C language advantage.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly (34.91 +/- 0.93x vs filtlong; 1.19x and 1.01x vs seqtk 1-pass and 2-pass). Shortcomings: the filtlong comparison measures a different algorithm, the like-for-like seqtk -2 result is parity, versions and toolchain are unpinned, and the runner CPU is not stated. tier_reason: A first-party harness (vectordotdev/vector-test-harness) with public Terraform/Ansible configs. The tcp_to_blackhole default configuration pins c5.large instances, but no CPU model, compiler or build flags are given, and the harness README says it is under construction and some performance tests may be broken. That makes it C.

corrections.baseline: Fluent Bit (C log forwarder): 1.1.0 in the TCP to Blackhole, File to TCP, TCP to HTTP and TCP to TCP rows, 3.2.7 in the Regex Parsing row. The same table lists Filebeat (Go), Fluentd and Logstash (Ruby/JVM) and the closed-source Splunk Universal and Heavy Forwarders, whose implementation language was not verified here.
corrections.hardware: AWS c5.large subject with 10 c5.large producers for tcp_to_blackhole (cases/tcp_to_blackhole_performance/configurations/default/terraform.tfvars); other cases' tfvars not checked; CPU model not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party harness, and the README says it is under construction and some performance tests may be broken. The rows mix vintages. TCP to Blackhole and TCP to HTTP compare fluentbit 1.1.0 with vector 0.2.0-6-g434bed8, and File to TCP (multi_file; the single_file results are empty) and TCP to TCP compare fluentbit 1.1.0 with vector 0.2.0, all from 2019. Only Regex Parsing was re-run with current versions (fluentbit 3.2.7, vector 0.55.0), and there Vector is 1.55x slower (13.2 vs 20.5 MiB/s, derived from page data). In TCP to Blackhole, Fluent Bit 1.1.0 peaks at 53.2 CPU usr against Vector's 96.5 on a 2-vCPU c5.large, which suggests Fluent Bit used about one core and Vector both (derived from page data). Splunk UF wins TCP to TCP (70.4 MiB/s). These are whole-product comparisons with different feature sets, and no compiler or flags are stated.
corrections.why_faster: Not attributable to the language. These are whole products, and the wins are against a 2019 Fluent Bit 1.1.0 that, judging by its CPU usage, ran on about one of the two vCPUs. The one case re-run against current Fluent Bit 3.2.7 (regex parsing) has Vector slower.

notes: README numbers match the case READMEs in vector-test-harness for all five rows: 1.34x, 2.2x and 1.36x wins (derived), parity at TCP to TCP, a loss on regex parsing. Main shortcomings: 2019 versions behind every winning row, the only current-version re-run is a loss, Fluent Bit 1.1.0 was probably CPU-limited to one core, and there is no CPU model or flags. tier_reason: The README numbers come from BENCHMARKS.md, which commit b82fa0c removed from master. It was read at commit 9b2c398 and is first-party. It names Apple Git 2.50.1 and git 2.43.0 but no exact CPU ("Apple M-series", "vers VM") or git build flags. The hyperfine scripts and the lib_bench.zig it cites are not in the repo: benchmarks/cli_benchmark.zig times different commands with its own timer and hard-codes /root/ziggit. So it is C, and the README claim is overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md (2026-03-31, commit 9b2c398). On macOS arm64 the small repo (51 commits) is 4.9x faster on average (status 8.1 vs 1.0 ms, 8.1x; log -20 5.0x; branch -a 5.6x; blame 1.3x) and the large repo (2,367 commits) 4.4x on average (status 2.1x, show --stat 1.2x, log --oneline all 1.4x, blame 36.0 vs 2.8 ms, 12.6x). On Linux x86_64 the small repo averages 1.2x (log -20 0.8x). On the large Linux repo ziggit is slower on 8 of 10 commands (status 0.7x, diff --stat 0.3x, show --stat 0.3x) and wins only blame (87.9 vs 7.9 ms, 11.1x). Library calls versus spawning git: findCommit 85.4x macOS and 6.3x Linux, cloneBare 7.3x and 34.3x, full workflow 9.6x (all 5 repos) and 32.4x. End-to-end bun install with the ziggit integration: 0.93-1.39x cold, parity warm. The README's '4-10x' headline mixes small-repo rows with the large-repo blame row and omits the Linux CLI results.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: ziggit: Zig 0.15.2, ReleaseFast. git: Apple Git 2.50.1 (macOS) and git 2.43.0 (Linux), build flags not stated. macOS CLI: hyperfine --warmup 5 --runs 100 (small repo) or --runs 50 (large repo). Linux CLI: shell loop with date +%s%N, 50 iterations. Library: a custom lib_bench.zig (not in the repo), 20 iterations.
corrections.hardware: Apple M-series arm64, macOS 15.6 (exact chip not stated); Linux x86_64 'vers VM' with 8 GB RAM (CPU model not stated).
corrections.caveats: First-party. The README headline cherry-picks: on Linux x86_64 the CLI averages 1.2x on a small repo, and on a large repo ziggit is slower on 8 of 10 commands (diff --stat and show --stat at 0.3x). The macOS gains are mostly git process launch, about 7-8 ms per invocation according to BENCHMARKS.md itself; the git binary path is not stated. Blame's 11-12.6x comes from in-process memoisation, and src/git/blame_cmd.zig has no rename detection, while git blame follows whole-file renames by default, so the work differs; output equivalence was not shown. The library rows time an in-process call against fork+exec of git; that is overhead, not implementation speed, and libgit2 would be the fair in-process baseline. The end-to-end bun install rows compare a ziggit-integrated bun 1.3.11-canary with stock bun 1.2.10 (different bun versions) and show only 0.93-1.39x. Succinct output is on by default in ziggit, so status/log print less than git. BENCHMARKS.md was removed from master (commit b82fa0c), and the benchmarks/*.zig in the repo do not reproduce the published tables.
corrections.why_faster: Process startup and in-process calls, not codegen. On macOS each git invocation costs about 7-8 ms against 1-2 ms for the static ziggit binary; on Linux, where spawn is about 2 ms, the advantage mostly disappears (1.2x small repo, slower on most large-repo commands). Blame wins through per-run memoisation without rename detection. Library rows avoid fork+exec entirely.

notes: README CLI numbers match BENCHMARKS.md, which is now removed from master and was read at commit 9b2c398. The README hides the Linux results, where ziggit is mostly at parity or slower, so the claim is downgraded as overstated, though the tier stays C. Shortcomings to record: startup-dominated microcommands, a cherry-picked headline, blame doing less work (no rename following), library rows that compare in-process calls with subprocess calls, E2E rows across different bun versions, and benchmark scripts missing from the repo.
